initial_observation.encounter_context: Presented initially to his pediatrician with left leg pain starting in July 2022
initial_observation.chief_complaint: Left leg pain progressing to inability to ambulate
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: Initial radiograph of knee and lower leg showed no fracture or deformity; pain worsened over months to limp and loss of weight bearing
presenting_symptoms: pain located on mid-anterior left thigh
unable to perform straight leg raise

evidence_items.source_text: A repeat radiograph of the hip revealed an ill-defined lytic lesion with pseudotrabeculation involving the proximal left femoral diaphysis extending into the femoral. Along with this, there was a lucency involving the inferior portion of the neck of the femur, which likely represents a pathologic fracture (Figure 1).
On admission, routine laboratory workups, including a complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, were within normal limits.

On physical exam, the lower left extremity showed no gross deformity, and motor movement and sensation to light touch were intact. Strength testing was 5/5 for knee extension and 4/5 for knee flexion. The patient’s pain was located on the mid-anterior left thigh, and he was unable to perform a straight leg raise.
Orthopedic surgery recommended magnetic resonance imaging to further characterize the lesion (Figure 2).
Pediatric orthopedic surgery biopsied the cystic lesion, and pathology revealed benign-appearing cystic tissue.

An open reduction and internal fixation with pins and a plate were completed for stabilization of the pathologic fracture (Figure 3). Curettage of the cyst was performed, and the cystic space was filled with an injectable inductive graft and crushed cancellous bone. Physical therapy and occupational therapy provided education for ambulation with a walker upon discharge post-operative day one.
Hematology/oncology followed the permanent pathology report, which ultimately diagnosed an aneurysmal bone cyst.
